letters.intro: The capital A is a favourite for monograms and initials — its wide, peaked shape fills a card front or a framed print beautifully. Puff the two legs out evenly and the whole letter reads like a little tent you can shade, stripe, or pattern. Print it big for a personalised A monogram, an initial on a place card, or the first letter of a name.
letters.draw: Start with a wide upside-down V, add the crossbar, then round every corner and puff the outline outward so the two legs look inflated.

letters.intro: A bold bubble B is a birthday-banner staple — think a big B pennant for a name or the start of BIRTHDAY strung across a wall. The two stacked bellies give you plenty of room to colour in blocks or stripes. Print several, cut them out, and punch holes to thread onto string.
letters.draw: Draw the tall spine, then two stacked D-curves; round the bumps and puff the outline so both bellies look like balloons.

letters.intro: The open curve of a bubble C is easy to cut out, which makes it a go-to for classroom door displays and letter-of-the-week boards. Its single sweep leaves a wide inside to fill with a pattern, a photo, or a child's name. Printed large, it still reads clearly as a header from across the room.
letters.draw: Draw a fat backwards C, then trace a second curve inside so you get a thick crescent, and round both tips.

letters.intro: A rounded bubble D anchors a poster or sign nicely — the straight spine keeps it steady while the big belly gives you a colourable panel. Use it as a drop-cap to open a word on a flyer, or blow it up as a single decorative letter. The clean outline stays crisp even at large print sizes.
letters.draw: Draw a straight spine, add one big half-circle belly, then puff the curve outward and round the two corners.

letters.intro: A bubble E makes a friendly bullet-journal header — three short rounded bars fill a spread title without crowding the page. Kept chunky, it doubles as a decorative drop-cap for the first word of a list or a weekly log. Sketch it in pencil first, then ink over the puffy outline.
letters.draw: Draw the spine, then three short arms; round every end and puff the outline so each bar looks softly inflated.

letters.intro: A bubble F is a neat scrapbook-title letter — it opens words like Family, Fun, and Friends that head up a photo page. The two arms leave open space to tuck in a small doodle or a date. Print it, colour it to match your paper, and glue it down as a title cap.
letters.draw: Draw the spine and two arms at the top and middle; round the ends and puff the outline outward on every stroke.

letters.intro: A round bubble G sits happily on a gift tag — its curl gives the tag a soft, hand-made feel next to a length of ribbon. The generous loop is easy to colour in a single bright shade or a gentle gradient. Print it small for tags, or large as a single-initial ornament.
letters.draw: Draw a fat C, then add the little inward shelf and hook; round the corners and puff the whole loop outward.

letters.intro: The bubble H opens HAPPY on nearly every birthday banner, so a puffy version always earns its keep at a party. Two thick posts and a bridge give you three panels to colour in different shades. Print a row of them, cut them out, and string them up above the table.
letters.draw: Draw two tall posts, join them with a bar, then round the corners and puff each post outward like a pillow.

letters.intro: A bubble I looks deceptively simple, but puffed up with serif caps it becomes a strong single letter for a poster or a tall sign. The slim body is quick to colour, and the top and bottom bars keep it from looking like a plain line. Print it tall for a doorway strip or an I-heart-you layout.
letters.draw: Draw a short vertical bar, add a cap and a foot, then round the corners and puff each edge so the whole letter looks chunky.

letters.intro: A bubble J makes a swooping monogram — the long hook gives an initial card real movement and a place to nest a small flourish. Its tail curves under the neighbouring letters in a name, so it pairs well in a two-letter monogram. Print it big and colour the hook in a single confident sweep.
letters.draw: Draw a long stem, curl it into a hook at the bottom, add the top cap, then round and puff the outline all the way round.

letters.intro: A bubble K is a sturdy pick for a locker or desk name tag — its two kicking arms make the letter feel active and easy to spot in a row of names. The angles give you separate panels to colour. Print it, laminate it, and stick it on a cubby, door, or backpack.
letters.draw: Draw the spine, then two arms meeting the middle; round each point and puff the outline so the arms look padded.

letters.intro: A bubble L is one of the easiest letters to cut out, which is why it turns up on classroom walls and word-wall headers. Its single corner leaves a big clean inside for a pattern or a photo. Printed large, it reads clearly as a header from the back of the room.
letters.draw: Draw a tall spine and a foot along the bottom, then round the corner and puff both strokes outward evenly.

letters.intro: The capital M is one of the most-requested monogram letters — its symmetrical peaks look balanced on a card front, a tote, or a framed initial. The two valleys give you four panels to colour or pattern. Print it big for a bold single-letter M monogram, or the start of a name.
letters.draw: Draw two tall posts, drop a V between them, then round every peak and valley and puff the outline outward.

letters.intro: A bubble N is a clean, readable choice for a name tag or a desk label — the diagonal keeps it lively without getting fussy. Its three strokes give distinct areas to colour. Print it, trim it, and pop it on a locker, cubby, or lunch box.
letters.draw: Draw two vertical posts, join them with a diagonal, then round the corners and puff each stroke like a balloon.

letters.intro: A perfectly round bubble O is a gift for a bullet-journal header — fill it with dots, a date, or a tiny scene and it becomes a decorative focal point on a spread. The ring is quick to ink and leaves a big colourable centre. Sketch the circle lightly first, then puff the band both ways.
letters.draw: Draw a circle, then a second circle inside it to make a ring, and round the band so it looks softly inflated.

letters.intro: A bubble P opens poster words like PARTY and PLAY, so it works hard as a display letter. The single top belly leaves the lower spine clean, which balances nicely at large sizes. Print it big as a drop-cap, or as a standalone decorative letter.
letters.draw: Draw a tall spine, add one belly at the top, then round the curve and puff the whole outline outward.

letters.intro: A bubble Q brings a little flourish to a gift tag — the round body plus a jaunty tail feels playful next to string and paper. The circle is easy to colour and the tail gives the tag a finished flick. Print it small for tags, or large as a quirky single initial.
letters.draw: Draw a fat O, add a short tail crossing the bottom-right, then round everything and puff the loop outward.

letters.intro: The capital R is a popular monogram initial — the belly and the kicking leg give it character on a card, a mug, or a framed print. Its three strokes make three panels to colour or pattern. Print it big for a bold R monogram, or the head of a name.
letters.draw: Draw the spine, add a top belly, then a leg kicking out; round each corner and puff the outline all around.

letters.intro: A curvy bubble S is a lovely scrapbook-title letter — it opens words like Summer, School, and Sweet that head up a memory page. Its double curve gives a flowing, ribbon-like shape to colour. Print it, match it to your paper, and glue it down as a title cap.
letters.draw: Draw a wiggly S, then trace a second curve alongside it to thicken the band, and round both tips.

letters.intro: A bubble T is a banner workhorse — it turns up in PARTY, CONGRATS, and countless strung-up words, so a puffy version is always handy. The wide cap and single post give you two clean areas to colour. Print a set, cut them out, and hang them on string.
letters.draw: Draw a wide top bar and a post dropping from its centre, then round the ends and puff both strokes outward.

letters.intro: A bubble U makes a soft, cup-shaped bullet-journal header — its open top invites a small doodle or a trailing vine on a spread. The single curve is quick to ink and leaves a roomy inside to colour. Sketch it lightly, then puff the outline on both sides.
letters.draw: Draw a wide U, then a second curve inside to thicken it, and round the bottom so it looks inflated.

letters.intro: A bubble V points the eye downward, which makes it a striking single letter on a poster or a V pennant. The two converging strokes give a bold, arrow-like shape that's easy to colour in two tones. Print it large for a decorative initial or a victory sign.
letters.draw: Draw a wide V, then a second V inside it to thicken the strokes, and round the point at the bottom.

letters.intro: A bubble W is a fun classroom letter — its zig-zag is eye-catching on a Welcome door sign or a word-wall header. The peaks and valleys give you four panels to colour in bright shades. Printed large, it holds attention from across the room.
letters.draw: Draw two side-by-side V shapes, then thicken each stroke and round the peaks and valleys so they look puffed.

letters.intro: A bubble X doubles as a kiss on a gift tag — pair it with an O for xoxo and it reads warm and hand-made. The crossing strokes make four little triangles you can colour separately. Print it small for tags, or large as a graphic single letter.
letters.draw: Draw a big cross of two diagonals, thicken each arm, then round the four tips and puff the outline outward.

letters.intro: A bubble Y is a handy scrapbook-title letter — it caps words like Yay, Yearbook, and You at the top of a photo page. The forked top and single stem give a friendly, open shape to colour. Print it, match your paper, and glue it down as a title letter.
letters.draw: Draw two short arms meeting a single stem, then thicken each stroke, round the fork, and puff the outline.

letters.intro: A bubble Z has a bold zig-zag that pops on a name tag or a locker label — it's easy to spot at the end of a row of names. Its three strokes give clear areas to colour in blocks. Print it, trim it, and stick it on a cubby, desk, or backpack.
letters.draw: Draw a top bar, a diagonal down to the left, and a bottom bar, then thicken each stroke and round the corners.
